column1: The Effects of the Pandemic on Market Power and Profitability

The thesis titled The Effects of the Pandemic on Market Power and Profitability by Juan Andres Espinosa-Torres and Jaime Ramirez-Cuellar  explores the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on firm-level markups and profit rates for a panel of 3 611 publicly traded firms in Compustat. The study finds that the average firm experienced increases in both markups and profit rates during the pandemic. The authors provide conditions to interpret these changes causally  suggesting what might have occurred had the pandemic not taken place. Their estimations indicate that without the pandemic  markups would have been 4% and 7% higher in 2020 and 2021  respectively  while profit rates would have been 2.1 and 6.4 percentage points lower. The study includes a series of tests to ensure the robustness of their approach and highlights significant heterogeneity in the pandemic's impact on firms  influenced by key firm characteristics and industry. Firms with lower than forecasted markups often had shorter stock-exchange tenures and fewer employees.

The introduction of the thesis emphasizes the pandemic's disruption of supply and demand across various markets  prompting an analysis of markup and profit rates from 2020 to 2021. The authors aim to document recent movements in these metrics and assess whether pre-pandemic trends could predict these changes or if the pandemic itself created conditions for increased market power. The paper contributes to the literature by documenting the increase in markups and profit rates  evaluating whether pre-pandemic trends predict these increases  and analyzing the heterogeneous effects of rising market power and profitability during the pandemic.

The authors use Bayesian structural time series models to forecast firm-level markups and profit rates  using data up to 2019. They find that the observed markup rate was lower than forecasted  while the profit rate was higher than expected. The study also examines the heterogeneous effects of the pandemic  noting that firms with lower markups during the pandemic were often newly publicly traded and had fewer employees. In contrast  there was low effect heterogeneity in profitability across firms with different employment levels  stock exchange tenure  or market share.

The thesis further analyzes industry-specific effects  finding that information  real estate  and chemical manufacturing experienced lower than expected markups  while warehousing and entertainment had higher markups. In terms of profit rates  transportation  entertainment  and hospitality performed poorly  whereas warehousing and real estate outperformed. These findings suggest an uneven impact of the pandemic on market power and profitability across firms.

To support their findings  the authors conduct a series of statistical tests to assess the efficacy of their Bayesian structural time series model in forecasting firm-level markup and profit rates. They test the model's assumptions  evaluate its accuracy in reflecting pre-pandemic data  and confirm the forecast quality for a pre-pandemic sample. Additionally  they perform robustness checks by considering alternative modeling choices and frameworks  such as varying hyperparameters in the Bayesian model and using local linear projections. Despite these changes  the main results remain consistent  reinforcing the reliability of their findings.

The results contribute to the literature on rising markups of publicly-traded firms in the US  extending previous analyses by providing evidence that pre-pandemic trends do not predict average market power behavior during the pandemic. The authors also uncover average behavior in markups and profitability  analyzing its heterogeneity by firm characteristics such as size  market share  and stock exchange tenure. They argue that their methods may provide a causal account of the pandemic's effects on markups and profit rates  supporting their identification strategy with the notion that pandemics are exogenous and unpredictable to the economy and firm dynamics.

The thesis concludes by situating its findings within the broader literature on the effects of the COVID-19 pandemic on macroeconomic aggregates  such as inflation  and the market power of firms. The authors highlight the importance of understanding these dynamics to inform policy and business strategy in the face of future disruptions.
